sentence: Opioids are prescribed for severe pain; the NHS lists constipation and drowsiness as common effects, and says the body can become used to them.
note: Morphine page: severe pain use; common side effects include constipation, sleepiness; tolerance explained in common questions.

sentence: The NHS describes opioids such as morphine, oxycodone and tramadol as prescription painkillers, with morphine used for severe pain after surgery, injury, cancer or at the end of life.
note: Morphine page: prescription-only opioid painkiller for severe pain such as after an operation, injury, cancer and end of life care. Oxycodone and tramadol described on the same basis in the NHS medicines pages (tramadol: TA).

sentence: Constipation and sleepiness are among the common side effects the NHS lists for opioids, and the NHS says the chance of side effects is greater at higher doses.
note: Side-effects pages list constipation, nausea, sleepiness, dizziness; higher dose raises the chance of side effects (morphine page).

sentence: The NHS says that with long-term use the body can become used to an opioid, which is called tolerance, and that addiction is possible.
note: Morphine and tramadol common-questions pages: body can get used to it (tolerance) so higher doses may be needed; possible to become addicted.

sentence: The NHS and NICE both say these medicines should not be stopped suddenly, because withdrawal symptoms can occur; the prescriber or pharmacist is the route to advice.
note: NHS morphine: do not stop suddenly, withdrawal possible, doctor reduces gradually. NICE NG215: opioids should not be stopped abruptly in most cases, slow stepwise reduction.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for slowed or difficult breathing or a seizure, and a GP is the usual first step for help with drug dependence.
note: Side effects of morphine page: call 999 for difficulty breathing or a seizure. Drug addiction getting help page: GP is usual first step.

sentence: Opioids are a group of strong painkillers, and they are available only on prescription.
note: Morphine page: prescription-only opioid painkiller for severe pain.

sentence: The NHS says morphine is used for severe pain, such as pain after an operation or an injury, pain from cancer, and pain at the end of life.
note: Morphine page: used to treat severe pain such as after an operation, injury, cancer and end of life care.

sentence: The NHS also describes tramadol and codeine as opioid painkillers.
note: Tramadol and codeine NHS pages describe them as opioid pain medicines (title/lead of each page).

sentence: Opioids work in the brain and nervous system, where they block pain signals travelling to the rest of the body and also reduce the anxiety and stress that pain causes.
note: About morphine page (as summarised on the site's own morphine entry): works in the central nervous system and brain to block pain signals and reduce anxiety and stress caused by pain.

sentence: Hospital leaflets say strong opioids are generally meant for short-term use.
note: Search summary of trust leaflets: strong opioids are generally for short-term use; long-term use not recommended.

sentence: Hospital pain leaflets often sort opioids into weak and strong groups.
note: Leeds Teaching Hospitals pain page: dihydrocodeine, codeine and tramadol listed as weak; morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl and buprenorphine as strong.

sentence: Leeds Teaching Hospitals places codeine, dihydrocodeine and tramadol in the weak group, and morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl and buprenorphine in the strong group.
note: Same Leeds page.

sentence: It describes weak opioids as aimed at mild to moderate pain, and strong opioids as for severe pain that simple painkillers have not relieved.
note: Leeds page: weak opioids for mild to moderate pain; strong ones for severe pain not relieved by simple painkillers.

sentence: The wording is not the same everywhere: another NHS trust leaflet lists tramadol as strong.
note: A West Hertfordshire-linked leaflet (https://www.westhertshospitals.nhs.uk/application/files/7517/3315/9897/44-2240-V4__Strong_Opioids_UPLOADv.pdf) lists tramadol as strong, per search summary; the Leeds page lists it as weak.

sentence: The NHS lists constipation, feeling or being sick, sleepiness, dizziness, confusion, headaches and itchy skin as common side effects of morphine.
note: Side effects of morphine page: constipation, nausea, sleepiness, dizziness, confusion, headaches, itchy skin or rash.

sentence: The NHS says the higher the dose, the greater the chance of side effects.
note: Morphine side effects page, per search summary.

sentence: Constipation happens because morphine slows digestion, and the NHS says the same about codeine, including in co-codamol.
note: NHS morphine page: slows digestion; co-codamol common questions: codeine can slow digestion and cause constipation.

sentence: NHS and hospital pages say eating more fibre and drinking more fluids may help, and a laxative is sometimes needed.
note: Hospital leaflets suggest fibre, fluids and a laxative if needed (search summary of trust leaflets); the laxative sentence is from trust leaflets rather than a national NHS page.

sentence: A pharmacist or GP can advise on constipation that does not settle.
note: Routing statement: persistent constipation to GP or pharmacist, from search summary; not a quoted NHS sentence.

sentence: Feeling sick usually wears off, but the NHS says that serious side effects, though rare, include an allergic reaction, changes to vision, an unusual heartbeat, and slowed or difficult breathing.
note: Morphine side effects page: nausea normally wears off; serious effects rare and include anaphylaxis, vision changes, breathing difficulties, unusual heartbeat.

sentence: The NHS says that if morphine or tramadol is taken for a long time, the body can become used to it, which is called tolerance.
note: Morphine and tramadol common questions pages: long-term use can lead to tolerance.

sentence: With tolerance, higher doses may be needed over time to control the same pain.
note: Same pages: higher doses may be needed.

sentence: The NHS also says it is possible to become addicted, and that the prescriber explains how to lower that risk.
note: Morphine common questions: possible to become addicted, doctor will explain how to reduce the risk; tramadol: possible to become addicted.

sentence: NICE guidance on medicines linked to dependence describes dependence as involving both tolerance and withdrawal symptoms, and notes that dependence alone does not rule out continued or new prescribing.
note: NG215 summary: defines dependence as involving tolerance and withdrawal symptoms; dependence is not in itself a contraindication to continued or new prescribing.

sentence: The Faculty of Pain Medicine, which runs the Opioids Aware resource for the UK, says there is not enough evidence about the long-term benefits of opioids for chronic pain, and that the risk of harm is higher.
note: FPM 'Opioids for long term pain': insufficient evidence to determine long-term benefits of opioid therapy for chronic pain, and increased risk of harms.

sentence: Its patient page says it is rare for people in pain to become addicted, while also noting that some people respond less well to opioids over a long period.
note: FPM information for patients: rare for people in pain to become addicted; some patients show a disappointing response over a long period.

sentence: NICE chronic pain guidance recommends against starting opioids for chronic primary pain, which is long-lasting pain without another underlying condition that explains it.
note: NG193 rationale: committee recommended against starting opioid treatment for chronic primary pain. The definition of chronic primary pain is added by the author as a plain-language gloss.

sentence: For tramadol, the NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol, because side effects such as sleepiness are more likely.
note: Tramadol common questions page: best not to drink alcohol with tramadol; more likely to get side effects like feeling sleepy.

sentence: For morphine, the NHS says alcohol can make a person sleepier and may raise the risk of serious side effects.
note: Search summary of NHS morphine pages: generally advises avoiding alcohol; may make you more sleepy or increase risk of serious side effects. Wording blends pages.

sentence: The NHS says not to drive or ride a bike if the medicine causes sleepiness, blurred vision, dizziness, clumsiness or trouble concentrating.
note: Morphine and tramadol NHS pages: don't drive, cycle or use machinery if sleepy, blurred vision, dizzy, clumsy or unable to concentrate.

sentence: The NHS says that recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin raise the risk of breathing problems with morphine.
note: Morphine NHS page, per search summary: cannabis, cocaine or heroin with morphine can lead to breathing difficulties, seizures and coma.

sentence: The NHS says to speak to the doctor before stopping morphine, because stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal symptoms.
note: Morphine NHS pages: stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal; consult doctor first.

sentence: It lists feeling agitated or anxious, trouble sleeping, sweating and restlessness as examples.
note: Search summary: withdrawal can include agitation or anxiety, difficulty sleeping, sweating, restlessness.

sentence: The NHS says the doctor then lowers the dose gradually over time.
note: Morphine NHS pages: doctor will gradually reduce the dose.

sentence: NICE says opioids should not be stopped abruptly in most cases, and describes a slow, stepwise reduction.
note: NG215 summary: slow stepwise reduction for opioids; should not be stopped abruptly in most cases.

sentence: The NHS tramadol page says the treatment plan may include details of how and when to stop.
note: Search summary: treatment plan may include details of how and when to stop tramadol.

sentence: The NHS says to speak to the doctor first, so the prescriber or a pharmacist is the route for questions about this.
note: Morphine NHS pages: consult the doctor before stopping; pharmacist as a route for medicine questions is general NHS signposting.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for slowed or difficult breathing or a seizure, and for signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as a swollen face, mouth, lips or throat.
note: Side effects of morphine page: call 999 for a seizure, difficulty breathing; anaphylaxis signs listed. The detail of a swollen face, throat or tongue comes from the site's own morphine entry citing the NHS.

sentence: Other serious effects, such as an unusual heartbeat or changes to vision, need prompt medical advice, and the NHS points to NHS 111 or a doctor for these.
note: Site's morphine entry: NHS advises reporting irregular heartbeat, blurred or double vision to a doctor or NHS 111.

sentence: For help with dependence on a medicine, the NHS says a GP is the usual first step and can discuss the problem and help arrange treatment.
note: Drug addiction: getting help page: GP can discuss problems and help get into treatment, usually referring to a local drug service.

sentence: The NHS adds that many drug treatment services accept self-referral, and that anyone needing help is entitled to treatment like anyone else with a health problem.
note: Same page.

sentence: The FRANK helpline is open every day on 0300 123 6600.
note: Search summary of NHS-linked pages; the number and hours were not individually confirmed on the nhs.uk page.

sentence: For urgent advice about side effects, the NHS points to NHS 111.
note: Morphine side effects page: report irregular heartbeat or vision changes to a doctor or NHS 111.
